Welcome back to another episode of TEN — Transport Evolved News. Thanks for joining me. I hope you are safe, well, and with someone you care about, who also cares for you.

The automotive world is full of oversized, overpriced pickups, so our first story is a welcome update on one of the two trucks challenging the idea that bigger is better: the Mini-Cooper-sized Telo MT1. This week, the firm exited an unusually quiet period spent completing impact and crash testing. With that done, Telo confirmed a partnership with Michigan’s Schwab Industries, which will produce the MT1’s body-in-white. CEO Jason Marks says more news is coming soon, but didn’t confirm final assembly or a build date. Telo did confirm the MT1 comes standard with a split 400-volt battery pack, letting it charge at both 400- and 800-volt stations. While Telo’s site still promises a 20-80% charge in 20 minutes, the new announcement floated sustained rates of up to 400 kilowatts, so if that holds in the real world, charging will be blisteringly quick.

One of the last bastions of the performance sedan, BMW has been working on its electric M3 for a while, and this week debuted the BMW M Concept Neue Klasse, revealed at the 24 Hours of Le Mans. It’s among the most powerful BMWs yet, and previews the production electric M3, due shortly. BMW is vague on some specs, but confirmed a quad-motor setup — one per wheel — and an 800-volt battery pack with over 100 kilowatt-hours capacity, built using specially tweaked, M-specific cylindrical cells for high power density and repeated high charge rates. Also new for BMW, the structural battery pack is integrated with both the front and rear axle, aiding chassis stiffness while cutting weight. We know from previous videos that BMW engineers and board members have been blown away, so let’s hope they let us drive it soon.

New Benchmark Mineral Intelligence data suggests May’s EV sales kept growing year-over-year around the globe, with 1.8 million new EVs registered. While the overall picture is good — global growth is 3% year-over-year and 7% month-over-month — North America’s market is down 26% year-over-year, while China’s fell 9%, though it still made up over one-half of all EVs sold. Happily, Europe and the rest of the world offset both declines, with year-to-date figures now at 7.5 million EVs. That optimism carries into Bloomberg New Energy Finance’s latest Electric Vehicle Outlook, which expects over 23 million new EVs sold by year’s end, up 11% on 2025, with over one-quarter of new cars all electric. That said, it is less rosy than before, caused — in my words, and not theirs — by the US federal government’s war on EVs.

I drive a lot of different vehicles for this job, and when it comes to performance cars, the Porsche Taycan is one of the best prestige performance EVs out there. And if you’re curious, the Kia EV6 GT is my all-time favorite performance EV. Part of what makes the Taycan so good is its devotion to road manners, power delivery, and seemingly never-ending grip. But this week, we learned Porsche is updating the 2027 Taycan in a way that eliminates some of that smoothness: E-Shift with virtual gears, a simulated rev counter, and faux engine noises. As other outlets noted, it’ll likely make the car slower and less refined to drive quickly, but happily, it’s user-configurable. More important to note, though, is the fact that NACS now comes as standard for DC fast charging in North America, though the driver’s-side AC port stays at J1772 — and the larger Performance Battery Plus pack is now standard across all models.

Regulars will know that we are vocal right-to-repair advocates who think everyone deserves to fix their own things, and we do everything we can to encourage you to learn, so keep your eyes peeled for a DIY video early next week. But as the Detroit Free Press reported this week, Ford and GM might disagree. Executives from Ford, GM, and Penske met at the White House earlier this month, and according to President Trump, the talks touched on a bill that would stop people from fixing their cars. The details stay vague, though Ford confirmed that Andrew Frick, president of Ford Blue and Model e, attended. Then Ford CEO Jim Farley made things worse. Speaking to the Free Press at an auto-technician training event, of all places, he argued that modern cars are too complex for enthusiasts to repair safely, even as he backs wrenching on older ones. He said DIY was fine except for warranty work, which is odd, since warranty repairs are free at the dealer anyway.

Sending things through the mail is one of the most traditional ways to get messages from one person to another, and in the digital age, it is often overlooked. But that doesn’t mean the world’s postal services are stuck in the past, and as regulars will know, we regularly cover delivery fleets transitioning to electric, from two-wheelers in Australia to HGVs in the UK, and more recently, An Post’s massive reduction in CO2 from its EV shift. This week, Austria’s national postal service, Österreichische Post AG, celebrated switching its Vienna fleet to all-electric, becoming Europe’s largest metropolitan area with a completely CO2-free postal service. To mark the milestone, an official event took place with Austrian native and former California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger. The transition is the result of a 32-million-euro investment by the company, and will serve as a model for future electric postal services across the nation.

BMW posted more teasers this week for its upcoming X5 SUV, a vehicle that will be available in multiple drivetrains, including battery electric and hydrogen fuel cell. In addition to detailing its new SAE Level 2 driver assistance system, BMW confirmed that the BMW iX5 60 xDrive, the range-topping electric variant of the X5, will come with a truly massive 800-volt battery pack with a usable capacity of 141 kWh in Europe and 144 kWh in North America. That’s larger than the 131 kWh of the now-discontinued Ford F-150 Lightning, and larger than most other EVs on the market today. BMW hasn’t given a range figure, but Electrek predicted this week it could top 500 miles — 805 kilometers — with careful driving, well beyond the normal bladder limit of a standard-issue human. And while that might convince skeptics to go electric, it does nothing to curb the pandemic of oversized, overweight EVs on our roads.

For some time, the UK, despite some of its other challenges and poor decision-making of late, has been making meaningful progress towards a transition to electric vehicles. But this week, we learned it’s reportedly about to abandon its plan requiring 80% of new cars sold to be electric by 2030, replacing it with a target that could be as low as 50%. The history is messy. Boris Johnson originally set a 2030 petrol and diesel ban, then Rishi Sunak pushed it to 2035, then Labour restored it, with the mandate topping out at 80% EV by 2030. But now embattled Prime Minister Starmer — facing backbench pressure and calls to resign, and amid heavy auto industry lobbying — looks about to cave. Last year, UK EV sales hit nearly a quarter of all new cars, so shifting the goalposts yet again is a poor choice. But then, the UK seems hell-bent on letting industry pressure push it into poor decisions that affect everyone.

I’m afraid the last two stories of this segment aren’t great if you are a fan of clean energy, because they do show the enshittification of the energy industry clearly. First, the US Department of the Interior announced a new deal with Invenergy that will see it terminate four of its offshore wind leases in exchange for a refund from the federal government totaling US$765 million. In its place, it will commit to new gas-powered plants in Indiana, Wisconsin, Iowa, Kansas, and Missouri, plus geothermal plants in western states. A bunch of misinformation accompanied the official press release, but it’s stuff we can see through: wind doesn’t work, isn’t reliable, etc., etc., etc. And if that wasn’t enough, Reuters reported last week that Shell is reportedly looking to sell off its wind farm assets in the US in a deal worth more than US$1 billion. We can all guess who’s calling the shots there.

Which brings me to the story most likely to get me death threats, because whenever I discuss this guy, the hate comes rolling in. As Elon Musk — often held up as the savior of the human race by his fans, and for years by EV drivers in general — has drifted ever further right, so has his approach to emissions. Add in environmental violations at Tesla and SpaceX facilities, plus his rockets and his private jet use, and it’s pretty grim. And this week he hit a new low. The US Department of Justice went into federal court on Musk’s behalf to get a Clean Air Act case against xAI, brought by the NAACP, thrown out. The facts are fairly simple. xAI is running 27 gas turbines without permits or pollution controls just over the Tennessee state line in Southaven, Mississippi, to power its Colossus data centers in Memphis, Tennessee. And they are likely now the single largest source of smog-forming pollution in a region with some of the worst asthma rates in the nation. The DOJ’s argument for throwing out the case against xAI? That making xAI follow the rules would threaten national, economic, and energy security. Yeah — the same argument used to kill wind farms is now defending heavy pollution. And worth sitting with is the fact that Musk spent over 250 million dollars getting the President re-elected, and the DOJ is now in court shielding his data center from environmental protection law. If you are watching this and are still making excuses for him, you’re probably someone pointing at your hat and asking, “Are we the baddies?”

Our recall reminders are next, but first, for several weeks now I’ve been telling you about the amazing EV raffle organized by our non-profit friends at the CCAN Action Fund. And not only is it an opportunity to get three chances to win a brand-new electric vehicle with every ticket, it’s a great opportunity to support a non-profit working to hold major fossil fuel polluters accountable for the climate crisis. We are now more than halfway through the raffle period, and there are still thousands of tickets left unsold. And as I just hinted, each ticket gets you not one, not two, but three chances to win a really great selection of some of the best EVs on the market today. The math is pretty simple: with fewer people buying tickets, your individual chances of winning are increased, especially with three potential chances to win per ticket. The first prize winner will build their own luxury Rivian, Lucid, or Porsche EV of up to 115 thousand dollars in value. Second prize will choose between the Rivian R2, Volkswagen ID. Buzz, or Hyundai Ioniq. And the third prize winner will win a Chevrolet Bolt. Tickets — every dollar supports the CCAN Action Fund’s work to shift the rising cost of climate-related disasters, like increased intensity of floods and wildfires, away from everyday people like you and I, and onto the largest, dirtiest energy polluters. And given some of the stories we’ve covered this week, I think you’ll agree we need amazing non-profits like the CCAN Action Fund. There are still plenty of tickets left, but time is running out, so to grab your tickets and support this amazing non-profit, head over to www.evraffle.org — that’s EV raffle dot org — or find the link in our show notes, or point your smart device at the on-screen QR code right here. Good luck.

And now it’s time for our recall reminders. This week, we’ve got multiple emails from NHTSA, some with week-old recalls in them. Oh joy. The Honda CR-V fuel cell plug-in hybrid is among several Honda models being recalled for a tire repair bottle cap that can become a projectile while being used. And apparently, FCV recalls are like buses, because the Toyota Mirai is among a number of Toyota vehicles recalled this week for an instrument panel display fault. Owners will be notified. International Motors is recalling some eVSB models for the second week in a row, this time to address a drive motor bolt that could come loose, causing a loss of power. And finally for the recalls, Waymo is recalling 3,800 robo-taxis after discovering its cars were failing to identify construction zones, leading them to behave like every other freaking driver and ignore posted speed limits, putting road workers at risk. And those are our recall reminders.

Now it’s time for our news shorts. As usual, you’ll find full links on our website at transportevolved.com.

Genesis has confirmed it’ll expand EV sales into four new countries next year — Austria, Denmark, Poland, and Portugal — after its Spanish launch late this year, reaching 11 European markets in total.

VinFast has signed a new deal in its home market of Vietnam, bringing up to 2,000 of its EVs to the Green SM ride-hail and taxi service via operator Huy Long.

A Reuters investigation accuses Tesla of giving European regulators misleading FSD safety data, including a comparison error inflating its safety claims threefold, though Dutch authorities say it didn’t affect approval.

BMW surprised many by opening the order books on Thursday for the new BMW i3, months ahead of planned schedule. BMW’s UK press portal published the First Edition from £57,905.

Rivian and ChargeScape have signed a partnership deal that will give Rivian owners the ability to enroll in smart charging programs, saving money and encouraging a greener grid.

UK-based firm Zenobē has secured £980 million in financing to help it accelerate the rollout of electric buses in both the UK and Ireland, funding 1,200 new electric buses.

Less than a week after launching the Rivian R2, Rivian has confirmed it’s laying off hundreds as it aims to narrow its losses. Less than 2% of its workforce are affected.

Renault Brazil has officially started production of the Geely EX2 EV for the domestic market. It’s the second model to be made by Renault Brazil for the Chinese automaker.

IAV and Nexperia have introduced the “ONE Inverter” concept. This concept is capable of bidirectional power transfer and utilizes gallium nitride and silicon carbide components to extract more power and energy from a given capacity battery pack.

Mercedes-Benz has officially begun production of its luxury VLE minivan. Marketed as having the luxury of an S-Class with the practicality of a minivan, its primary customers will be limousine fleets.

Stellantis has officially priced the e-208 GTi in several markets in Europe, including the UK. It will start in the UK from a highly competitive £34,995 in the hot-hatch segment.

Charging network Galp has successfully completed a new corridor of fast charging, connecting Porto to the Algarve in Portugal. In total, 20 megawatts of installed power exists on the network.

Škoda has published details of more than 1.5 million kilometers of road testing carried out on its soon-to-launch Škoda Peaq. The car’s premiere will take place next week.

Transport for London now has more than 3,000 electric buses in its fleet. According to the operator, the buses have saved an estimated 100,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions per year.

Edenred will be purchasing The Mobility House’s fleet charging business. The sale, due in the third quarter, allows The Mobility House to focus on V2G as its core business.

CATL’s CEO stated this week that pure solid-state batteries in EVs are still several years away from mass adoption, with mass-market commercialization by 2030 unlikely.

Kyiv, Ukraine, is installing 6,500 new EV charging stations despite ongoing Russian aggression. EVs can be charged from various power sources, making them very versatile for war zones.

Fastned, in partnership with Places for London, has launched a 12-bay ultra-rapid EV charging station at Hatton Cross. It’s the first of 25 planned sites to open under the partnership.

XPeng has officially launched its X9 MPV in select European markets. Customers can now order one in Germany, Finland, Norway, Iceland, Croatia, Slovenia, and Hungary.

Renault and Continental have unveiled a new jointly developed EV tire with a 35% lower rolling resistance than the EU “A” rating. It’s claimed to offer significant range boosts per charge.

BYD has scaled up its battery production in Brazil as part of a significant investment into the region. BYD aims to reach 50% local content in its Brazilian-made EVs by next year.

German parts company Autohelden plans to start importing various Chinese EVs, including Xiaomi, Zeekr, and XPeng, directly into the EU. Other firms are also planning similar import services.

Shillong, the capital of Meghalaya, India, has introduced its first five electric buses thanks to the Indian government’s nationwide PM e-Bus Sewa scheme.

Researchers at the Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg in Germany have used recycled tire particles to reduce noise and vibration in EV power electronics, making EV travel even quieter.

Nissan is rebranding its Chinese-market N7 EV for the Philippines, where it will be known as the Primera EV. It will be sold alongside the new Nissan Navara plug-in hybrid.

Microlino is going to court in Switzerland to argue for equal treatment with full-size EVs under CO2 fleet rules, since its bubble cars currently don’t classify as fully-fledged EVs.

California’s transportation department, Caltrans, has ordered another 524 Rivian vehicles for its fleet. Once delivered, it will operate nearly 1,000 Rivian-made vehicles in its maintenance fleet.

Chinese firm Bontu is bringing three all-electric quadricycles to Europe: the BTE05 and BTE09 microcars, and the BTE03 electric truck — which is heccing cute.

Norwegian maritime investment group Eitzen is building two new all-electric container vessels with a Chinese shipbuilder. They’re due to arrive in the region in the next three years.

BP Pulse has announced a loyalty program with IAG Loyalty, letting UK customers collect points while charging. And as the late Bruce Forsyth used to say, points mean prizes!

Xiaomi has unveiled a home robotic arm for plugging in your EV, more than a decade after Tesla promised such a product but never commercialized it.

Swedish company ElonRoad — no relation to Elon Musk — has added a second electric terminal tractor to its conductive charging-rail program at the Kalmar Innovation Centre. It works like a giant slot car.

Nio has officially updated the Champion Edition versions of its ET5, ET5 Touring, and EC6, adding 100 kilowatt-hour batteries and some notable performance tweaks.

Scania has signed a deal with transport firm Wibax to supply 105 all-electric trucks for haulage duties across Europe. The two firms have worked together on EVs since 2022.

The Swiss government has approved a Level 4 autonomous driving permit for AmiGo, a service run by Baidu’s Apollo Go and Swiss PostBus.

A US District Court judge has overturned the IRS’s attempt to scrap the 5% safe-harbor rule, which let solar projects that started construction before the tax credit expiry still claim some credits, even if completed afterwards.

A cottage industry is growing on Chinese e-commerce platforms selling fake heads designed to trick Tesla’s FSD system into thinking drivers are paying attention when they’re not.

New S&P Global Mobility data shows Toyota’s US EV registrations soared 225% in April, outselling BMW, Kia, Honda, Nissan, Lucid, Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen, and Volvo for that month.

Ford has begun producing low-cost LFP battery cells for its future universal EV platform, including the yet-to-launch US$30,000 pickup currently in testing.

BYD has officially opened orders for its Great Tang SUV in China, already hitting 150,000 pre-orders, helped by a starting price equivalent to around US$35,500.

Lucid has registered the design of its Cosmos crossover with the EU’s IP office, giving the first proper look at its next EV. It targets 300 miles of range from a 69 kWh battery.

The Port of Vancouver in Canada has launched an electric semi-truck pilot using Peterbilt 579 EV Class 8 trucks for drayage duties.

Honda and QuantumScape have announced a partnership to accelerate development of QuantumScape’s solid-state battery for future EVs.

Austrian battery diagnostics specialist Aviloo has announced a new warranty pledge. If a tested vehicle’s battery falls below its calculated limit, the owner gets up to €3,000 in compensation.

And finally for the news shorts, Candela has launched its most luxurious vehicle yet, the P-12 hydrofoil. Aimed at luxury resorts and the hyper-wealthy, the P-12 Voyager is built bespoke to customer specs.

And those are your news shorts — there will be more next week.

Our final two stories are coming right up, but first, a word on how we do what we do. Transport Evolved has been around for 15 years, and we’ve always believed that good information should be free — not paywalled, not driven by advertorials, and not beholden to anyone with a checkbook. That hasn’t changed, but what has changed is the financial landscape around us. YouTube ad revenue no longer covers our costs, and like a lot of indie creators, we’re feeling the squeeze. This month, that squeeze got a little tighter, as my partner, Kate, was laid off as part of a “corporate restructuring,” and as a small team where every dollar counts, that has a very real impact on what we’re able to do here. Kate’s income paid our household bills, and with that gone, I need to start pulling a salary from TE, but we can’t do that without a substantial increase in income. I hope, if able, you’ll consider helping us on that path — from $1.50 a month, making a one-off donation, or by visiting our swag store. Or perhaps, if you’re in the US, you’d consider using one of our long-time channel sponsors, EnergySage. They’re a great way to get trustworthy, verified solar experts helping you navigate the often complex process of getting solar panels for your own home — I personally used them for my own home, so I can vouch for their awesomeness. And if you choose them — whether for solar panels, a heat pump, or just to join a local community solar program, which is perfect for renters — we’ll receive a small referral fee. Supporting us would really mean a lot, and you could also be weaning off big energy bills at the same time. However you do it, thanks for your continued support.

And now it’s time for our final two stories.

We’ve covered the plethora of e-bike rules, and in the US alone, things are equally complex between different states. This week, New Jersey — due to implement new rules on July 19th, requiring all e-bikes be registered and riders licensed — is seeing a rising backlash. In just a few weeks, several thousand letters have been sent to the state opposing the rule, with advocates saying it’s created confusion and fear among riders, and even the state is unsure about enforcement. Meanwhile, in neighboring Washington, just down the road from me, reporting on tweaked e-bike rules is causing panic, with local outlets claiming they make Class 3 e-bikes legally motorcycles. But that’s not the case. The change simply clarified ambiguity over throttle use. If a bike with a throttle alone can hit 20 miles per hour, it’s not allowed. But an e-bicycle with pedal assist is still legal to that very same speed.

And finally, as one of the world’s quickest-charging vehicles, the new Denza Z9 GT from BYD is already proving popular in its launch market thanks to its range, recharging speed, and onboard tech. But to show just how versatile it is, BYD has waved off a brand-new Z9 GT on a 43-day, 9,300-mile road trip from Rome to Hong Kong. Called the Marco Polo Drive, it’ll be driven by Patrick Zhong, founding managing partner of M31 Capital, and Professor Jeffrey Sachs, director of Columbia University’s Center for Sustainable Development. The Z9 GT can manage more than 600 miles on the CLTC cycle, so some back-of-the-napkin maths suggests it should only need to charge around 16 times to reach its destination. But as with all long-distance travel, plenty of unknowns lie ahead. I hope the car and its occupants arrive in one piece, and good luck to all involved.

And on that note, we’re done for today’s show. But first, a massive thank you to the Electric Vehicle Association for sponsoring us. The EVA has been around since 1967 and is firmly committed to a cleaner, greener future for everyone. Join the EVA today, become an EV educator, and find ways to accelerate electric. If you haven’t made the switch yet, head over to myeva.org for more info. And thanks go to CCAN Action Fund. Tickets are just two hundred dollars, only ten thousand are being sold, and each ticket gets you three chances to win a brand-new EV. So don’t hang about. Grab your ticket today at EVRaffle.org. And thanks as well go to EnergySage. Follow the link below to start planning your energy-independent future today.

And of course, thank you. If you’re able, please consider supporting us using one of the methods I mentioned earlier in the show. Supporting us can also mean sharing our content, joining our Fluxr or Discord communities, promoting us on social media, or using our affiliate links, all of which are listed below. And if you are new to the channel, hi! Please give us a sub, either on YouTube or over on PeerTube.

Finally, you matter. You’re important. And while you might not always feel it, your voice and actions are important. I know it’s hard in a world filled with hate to feel like you have a place, but I want you to know that you do have one. The fact that you are here watching this means a lot to both myself and the team, and we are so very grateful that you are here, and that you are you. The world is scary right now. The news headlines are almost too much to bear at times. But remember that even the strongest people need time to reset — so do not be afraid to do that. Don’t be afraid to speak your truth. Take your time, listen to your own heart, and progress the world. And that world that we can build together is much stronger when we all have a voice, when we all listen, and when everyone is welcome. A cleaner, greener, safer, smarter, and more equitable world must be one rooted in justice, fairness, and a shared goal. So until next time, be your authentic self — whoever you are, wherever you are, and whoever you love. You are all part of this wonderful journey we are on together. As always, keep evolving.

text:
Energy companies are increasingly collaborating with technological entities, which is a testament to how both industries are growing simultaneously. Interestingly, both the technology and energy industries are heavily influencing each other. On the one hand, energy companies are integrating technology to build some of the most sophisticated facilities. On the other hand, technology entities require more electricity supply as artificial intelligence is growing at an unprecedented rate. In furtherance of this relationship, Zelestra secured an additional Texas solar offtake agreement with Meta covering 180 MW of generation capacity.

Zelestra collaborates with Meta for a 180 MW solar energy facility

Zelestra is a global, customer-oriented renewable energy company that develops, builds, and operates multi-technology clean energy solutions, including solar, wind, and battery storage. It is headquartered in Spain and supported by the private equity firm EQT. Zelestra is one of the companies that has maintained relevance over many generations after being founded in 2005.

Meta and renewable energy developer Zelestra have expanded their clean energy partnership with a new long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) connected to the 180 MWdc Palmera Solar Plant in Texas. The agreement represents yet another major step in Meta’s strategy to power its growing digital infrastructure with renewable electricity.

With countries going through the green revolution at the moment, it is important that companies that use an enormous amount of electricity use clean energy so that decarbonization targets can be met. Situated in Freestone County, the Palmera project enhances what is already a solid collaboration between the two companies.

Assessing the significance of the Meta and Zelestra collaboration for solar development

Interestingly, the two companies have an extended history of working with each other to execute some of the most unique initiatives. The latest agreement is one that displays increasing demand for utility-scale solar generation as technology entities are actively investing greatly in data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Through Palmera, Zelestra, and Meta further elevate their joint renewable energy portfolio that now occupies multiple states and reflects one of the largest corporate clean energy partnerships in the United States. The new agreement gives Meta access to the output of the 180 MWdc (140 MWac) Palmera Solar Plant, which is being developed in Freestone County, Texas.

There is great excitement surrounding the initiative as it is expected to contribute renewable electricity to the Texas grid while assisting Meta in progressing its commitment to matching its operations with 100% clean energy. In the earlier part of the year, Zelestra launched construction on the 176 MWdc Skull Creek Solar Plant in Texas and the 200 MWdc Reclamation Solar Project in Indiana.

Simultaneously, the 81 MWdc Jasper County Solar Project in Indiana has entered full commercial operation, becoming the first completed project under the collaboration.

Understanding the significance of the agreement for Meta and its objectives

Zelestra and Meta are leading by example and creating a replicable blueprint. The Palmera agreement means that Meta and Zelestra now have eight solar PPAs across the United States, which is reflective of an estimated 1.4 GWdc of contracted generation capacity that is expected to be operational by 2028.

Amanda Yang, who is Meta’s Head of Clean and Renewable Energy, stated the following:

“Meta is committed to bringing new renewable energy to the grid, and our expanding relationship with Zelestra is helping make that possible at scale. These projects aren’t just advancing our energy goals.”

Understanding Texas as a large-scale solar development hub in the U.S.

The latest initiative between the companies continues the pattern of Texas being one of the most active renewable energy markets in North America. Among the reasons why it has achieved this is that it has extensive solar energy resources, transmission infrastructure, and growing electricity demand.

text:
When Katy Cornell, a House candidate in Washington’s 26th Legislative District, went door to door, she heard one issue over and over: skyrocketing energy bills.

Cornell told “The Jake and Spike Show” on KIRO Newsradio that state climate mandates are driving up costs.

“The Clean Energy Transformation Act is the one that they’re pushing us to be at zero emissions by 2030,

net neutral carbon emissions,” she said. “So essentially they’re requiring all of our energy companies to switch over by 2030, and this requires billions of dollars in investment, and you’re talking transmission investment, the storage for this type of energy, converting over to different energy sources, and that is all being passed on to us, the consumer.”

Energy bills could rise 30% a year under current climate mandates

KIRO host Spike O’Neill asked Cornell if she wanted to revoke the policies or just push them to a more realistic timeframe.

“I think we all want to protect our beautiful state. It’s one of the most beautiful places on earth. All the goals are great; we just have to be realistic in how we can get there and how much we’re willing to pay for that — especially when we say we care the most about working families, because they’re the ones paying the real price,” Cornell responded. “They’re hurting really badly. The electric companies are saying energy rate bills are going to go up 30% a year.”

“I mean, that’s going to double your electricity bills in the next three years,” she continued. “Who can afford that? Nobody. Some people in Port Orchard are saying they’re paying already $700 to $800 a month for a three-bedroom house. I mean, you’re talking possibly $1,400.”

Cornell’s plan, if elected, is to extend the timeline from 2030 to around 2035 to 2040.

“That would allow us to decrease those bills, instead of going up 30%, they can go up maybe 10% a year, 5% a year, but it has to go up at a rate that wages go up, that people can adjust to that, if it goes up too drastically, we’re not going to be able to afford electricity,” she said.

description:
In the heart of the Emma community just outside Asheville, North Carolina, a transformation is taking place that goes far beyond hardwire and wires.
While the transition to renewable energy is often seen as a luxury, a partnership between Sugar Hollow Solar, PODER Emma, and Footprint Project is providing clean energy as a vital tool for innovative community resilience and displacement prevention.
This partnership with Sugar Hollow Solar and Footprint Project introduces a new layer of security: energy independence.
As Asheville looks toward a more sustainable future, the collaboration between Sugar Hollow Solar, PODER Emma and Footprint Project stands as a blueprint for equitable energy.

text:

In the heart of the Emma community just outside Asheville, North Carolina, a transformation is taking place that goes far beyond hardwire and wires. While the transition to renewable energy is often seen as a luxury, a partnership between Sugar Hollow Solar, PODER Emma, and Footprint Project is providing clean energy as a vital tool for innovative community resilience and displacement prevention.

The trio of organizations recently completed an array of solar installations that represent a significant leap forward in combining affordable housing preservation with environmental justice.

PODER Emma, a mobile home community, has long served as a resource for locals, utilizing cooperative ownership to protect families from displacement. By securing land collectively, they ensure that legacy residents who built the Emma neighborhood get to remain. This partnership with Sugar Hollow Solar and Footprint Project introduces a new layer of security: energy independence. By generating their own power, these communities are no longer at the mercy of rising utility rates, allowing financial resources to remain within the neighborhood.

“We are excited to take this step for clean energy,” said Alan Ramirez, Board Member and Secretary of La Esperanza, the real estate co-op for PODER Emma. “During the hurricane, La Esperanza was our hub for resources and resilience. With solar power, we are saving our resources, producing power and feeling stronger than ever.”

Fifteen solar panels were installed on custom-built porch roof structures for the mobile homes and a 46-kW system was installed on the roof of PODER’s community hub. These projects were made possible by the Repower WNC Fund, a Sugar Hollow Solar initiative supported by the Amicus Solar Cooperative, sub-grants for equipment and labor and PV panel donations by Footprint Project, donations by IronRidge and Invest Appalachia grants.

As Asheville looks toward a more sustainable future, the collaboration between Sugar Hollow Solar, PODER Emma and Footprint Project stands as a blueprint for equitable energy. Communities impacted by development are often left out of the entire process. These projects have helped highlight that when a community is given the information and tools needed, brilliant and innovative things can happen. By addressing the disproportionate percentage of income spent on utilities in lower-income communities, PODER Emma ensures that the Emma community remains in a place where they can thrive.

title: Toyota refused to chase EVs like everyone else—and it won the long game - How-To Geek
authors: Joe Kucinski, Tyler Dupont, Carl Anthony
description:
Americans love Toyota hybrids Five Toyota models rank among the most-driven hybrids At the top of the hybrid leaderboard is the Toyota Sienna minivan with an average of 17,368 miles driven annually.
People trust Toyota hybrids.
Yet on the flip side of the coin, Toyota’s luxury division, Lexus, dominates the list of the least driven conventional hybrids.
The second-least-driven conventional hybrid is the Lexus UX 250h; the RX 450h and the ES 300h round out the top four.
According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, sales of traditional hybrid vehicles continue to soar.
text:
A lot of people owe Toyota an apology. For years, the Japanese automaker has faced criticism for refusing to fully embrace the “electric vehicle revolution.”

While rivals raced to launch dozens of battery-electric models, Toyota continued investing heavily in conventional hybrid technology. Critics argued the company was moving too slowly and risking its future by not following the same path as competitors. For example, a 2021 Forbes article suggested that Toyota could be shooting itself in the foot by focusing more on hybrids than on battery-electric vehicles.

Coming off its best sales year ever in 2025, Toyota continues its streak as the world's best-selling automaker for the sixth consecutive year. If you want even more proof that Toyota got it right, all you need to do is reference the latest iSeeCars study, which shows that traditional hybrids are driven more than gasoline, plug-in hybrids, or EVs. And within the conventional hybrid segment, five of the top 10 most driven models are Toyota’s. That includes the top three.

The iSeeCars study reviewed more than 2.1 million three-year-old used vehicles sold in 2025. It showed that conventional hybrids are now the most heavily driven vehicles on American roads. On average, hybrids rack up 14,696 miles per year, more than all other drivetrain options.

Americans love Toyota hybrids

Five Toyota models rank among the most-driven hybrids

At the top of the hybrid leaderboard is the Toyota Sienna minivan with an average of 17,368 miles driven annually. That's 18.2% above the average hybrid and more than 4,000 miles higher than the average gasoline vehicle. In the number two spot is the Toyota Highlander Hybrid at 16,795 miles per year, followed by the Toyota Camry Hybrid at 16,605 miles.

Toyota's dominance continues, with the Corolla Hybrid taking the fifth-place spot, with 16,051 miles driven annually. And coming in at number 10 is the most famous hybrid of all, the Toyota Prius, with 15,088 annual miles.

The ultimate hybrid car

The Prius helped build Toyota's hybrid credibility

The Prius is a major reason Toyota hybrids are driven more than those of any other brand. Toyota spent decades refining its hybrid system. The company launched the original Prius in the United States more than 25 years ago, and since then, millions of hybrid Toyotas have accumulated billions of miles around the globe. People trust Toyota hybrids.

Toyota has built an unmatched reputation in this area, and the latest data suggests owners are taking full advantage of that peace of mind. People are not going to rack up more than 17,000 miles a year on a vehicle that they don’t trust, or one that spends a lot of time in the repair shop.

The other side of the coin

Toyota and Lexus hybrid owners use their vehicles in different ways

Toyota builds many of the most driven conventional hybrids. Yet on the flip side of the coin, Toyota’s luxury division, Lexus, dominates the list of the least driven conventional hybrids. The Lexus NX 350h is driven an average of just 10,312 miles per year, 29.8% below average. The second-least-driven conventional hybrid is the Lexus UX 250h; the RX 450h and the ES 300h round out the top four.

Buyers don’t seem to use luxury hybrid vehicles in the same way as mainstream hybrids. “Luxury hybrids appear to serve a different use case than mainstream hybrids, with buyers driving them substantially fewer miles per year,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer.

The Sweet spot between gas and EVs

Traditional hybrids offer the best of both worlds

Many people are not yet ready to make the switch to a fully electric vehicle or even a plug-in hybrid. However, nearly everyone is looking to reduce fuel consumption given the high price of gasoline. The traditional hybrid is perfect for these buyers.

Unlike EVs, conventional hybrids don't require charging infrastructure. Owners simply fill up at a gas station and continue driving. There is no need to plan routes around charging stations or adjust travel habits. At the same time, hybrids offer substantially better fuel economy than traditional gasoline vehicles.

A 2026 Toyota Corolla Hybrid has a combined fuel economy rating of 50 mpg. A gasoline-powered Toyota Corolla has a combined fuel economy rating of 34 mpg. According to the EPA, the Corolla Hybrid will save the owner $3,000 in gasoline costs over five years. That is a substantial amount of money, and those savings will continue year after year.

Toyota's long game appears to be paying off

For years, industry observers questioned Toyota's cautious approach toward electrification. Yet this study suggests that conventional hybrids remain incredibly important to American consumers. Toyota recognized early that many buyers wanted improved efficiency without changing established driving habits. Rather than forcing customers to adapt to new charging routines, Toyota offered familiar vehicles with dramatically better fuel economy.

The strategy appears to be resonating. Toyota is one of the few automakers that is not losing billions of dollars as it rethinks its EV strategy. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, sales of traditional hybrid vehicles continue to soar. Sales of EVs have fallen sharply since tax credits expired at the end of September last year.

If Americans continue driving Toyota hybrids more than any other vehicle, the company's decision to prioritize hybrids alongside EVs may ultimately prove to be one of the smartest moves in the modern automotive era.

text:
An abandoned 250-megawatt data center plan in Wake County, North Carolina, looks increasingly like part of a broader pattern rather than a standalone fight. Across the United States, opposition in the first quarter of 2026 helped delay or cancel data center projects worth more than $130 billion.

What happened?

According to Fortune, concerns about water use, air quality, and utility costs drove local resistance to Natelli Investments' proposed 190-acre data center campus. Earlier this year, after zoning changes, the developer withdrew its annexation and rezoning requests.

The dispute reflects a national trend identified by Data Center Watch: Seventy-five projects worth more than $130 billion were delayed or canceled in the first quarter, and active opposition groups grew from 396 at the end of 2025 to 833 by the end of March across 49 states.

The report said the pushback has spread beyond traditional tech hubs such as Northern Virginia and Northern California, with hearings and town meetings becoming more contentious as some states weigh or adopt moratoriums on large data center permits.

Why does it matter?

Data centers are central to the rapid acceleration of artificial intelligence technology. However, the infrastructure supporting them can require enormous amounts of electricity and water, raising concerns about air pollution, security risks, misuse, and unintended consequences such as higher household energy bills.

Fortune reported that a Heatmap Pro poll found that 70% of Americans do not want data centers built close to their homes.

Meanwhile, studies cited in the report project that wholesale electricity costs could rise by 6% to 29% by the end of the decade because of data center expansion, while the environmental and public health costs tied to AI infrastructure growth could reach $25 billion annually.

Utilities are already dealing with an aging grid, and JPMorgan Chase estimates $5.8 trillion in global grid upgrades over the next decade, including more than $1 trillion in the U.S.

Even when projects promise jobs and tax revenue, communities are increasingly asking who will bear the cost of the added strain.

What are people saying?

According to Fortune, resident Lorraine McAvoy summed up one of the biggest fears last year when she told WRAL News: "When they make infrastructure improvements, who does that cost go to? It doesn't go to the developer. It goes to the people, the consumers of the utility."

Miquel Vila, lead researcher at Data Center Watch, said, "Opposition to data centers — it's now part of a mainstream conversation. … We might see more of these fights escalate to a more legal front."

The Data Center Watch report put it even more starkly, stating, "In some cases, opposition mobilized before any project was officially filed; the mere rumor of a data center was enough to trigger organized resistance."

text:
I think we can all agree, no matter who we are, that high gas prices suuuuuuuuck. There is seemingly no benefit to paying, like, $70 to fill a Corolla. However, there may be a silver lining.

A recent report by Automotive News revealed that General Motors is starting to grow concerned with the industry’s obsession with expensive pickups and SUVs. Especially now that gas prices are so high. Filling up these oversized vehicles is nearly impossible for many American families.

“I’m not going to sit here and say it’s permanent yet,” GM North America President Duncan Aldred said at a Center for Automotive Research conference near Detroit. “But we are seeing somewhat of a shrinking of pickup trucks, full-size utilities, and some of the heavier [vehicles] and an increase in the more affordable segments of the industry.”

In the past, gas prices needed to be higher for six months or more to start such a dramatic shift towards fuel-efficient vehicles. But GM CEO Paul Jacobson felt it was a bit different this time around. He started to notice the shift over the last 12 weeks as gas prices reach nearly $5 a gallon. Gas prices may drop if the agreement between the U.S. and Iran is legit, although the drop would be gradual (if President Donald Trump even stuck to this).

If gas prices lowered, would Americans go back to their big, ugly, overpriced SUVs? It’s possible. But with the future so uncertain and policies changing by the moment, families may be hesitant to make such a large investment. The average price of a new vehicle is over $50,000 in the United States, and large pickups and SUVs are definitely part of the rising average.

Could small cars be coming back?

Nissan’s conflicting small car plans for the United States

Unfortunately, it’s never that simple. Even though Americans have been begging for small, cheap cars for years, automakers are hesitant. They’ve seen fewer buyers over the years, but this is due more to rising prices than to a lack of interest. Still, if Americans can’t afford the new norm for a compact car, it may not be worth making them. Why? Profit margin is much smaller for these more affordable vehicles.

However, some automakers have decided to take the plunge as the EV market declines. For under $30,000, you can get a Honda Civic, Toyota Corolla, Mazda3, Kia K4… Another brand is Nissan, which offers the Kicks for under $23,000 (base model). This subcompact crossover SUV is in the spotlight right now since Nissan recently revealed the Kicks e-Power.

Bad news for Americans: this version of the Kicks is only available in Japan. With a 1.4-liter three-cylinder engine that serves as a generator that charges the vehicle’s batteries, the Kicks e-Power has more torque than the U.S. model. But even more tantalizing: it’s just $18,700. America hasn’t seen a vehicle below $20,000 in years. Which is unfortunate, because it would likely sell insanely well in the current economy. If the e-Power comes to the U.S., the price will go up.

title: Is India Trading Its Reliance on Imported Oil With EV Batteries? - The Wire
description:
India currently imports nearly 89% of its crude oil requirements, and the dependence on oil imports is unlikely to decline significantly even in the long term.
However, India also imports over 90% of its lithium-ion cells, along with lithium and cobalt, for manufacturing EV batteries.
Does this mean India risks trading its dependence on imported oil for a new reliance on imported battery cells and minerals?
Oil dependence is continuous; battery dependence is largely upfront and can decline over time.
Battery minerals are circular Oil, once burnt, is gone, but battery minerals can be recovered.
text:
The ongoing West Asian supply chain disruptions have exposed a major vulnerability – over 96% of India’s 350 million vehicles run on imported petrol or diesel. India currently imports nearly 89% of its crude oil requirements, and the dependence on oil imports is unlikely to decline significantly even in the long term.

This has renewed calls to cut fuel use and accelerate electric vehicle (EV) adoption, further reinforced by the prime minister's recent calls for austerity. However, India also imports over 90% of its lithium-ion cells, along with lithium and cobalt, for manufacturing EV batteries.

Does this mean India risks trading its dependence on imported oil for a new reliance on imported battery cells and minerals? Yes, but it is a risk worth taking.

Why is this trade-off more strategic?

The answer lies in the difference between the dependencies: Conventional vehicles are built in India but run on imported fuel, whereas EVs rely on imported components but run on domestically generated electricity. Oil dependence is continuous; battery dependence is largely upfront and can decline over time. Neither is a perfect solution, but EVs offer a strategic form of dependence.

Why EV dependence is different

The battery cost is falling

Crude oil prices are shaped by the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries' decisions and geopolitical tensions, while battery prices depend more on Chinese industrial policy and supply chain control. The key difference is in the trend: crude has become about 70% more expensive over the past decade, whereas battery pack prices have fallen by around 60%.

Battery minerals are circular

Oil, once burnt, is gone, but battery minerals can be recovered. After 8–10 years ( average battery life), batteries can be reused, repurposed, and recycled. Driven by the National Critical Minerals Mission and the Battery Waste Management Rules, India’s battery circularity ecosystem is rapidly emerging. Recent studies have estimated that by 2030, recycling alone could meet 40%-50% of India's total EV battery mineral demand, significantly reducing the dependence on China.

Battery mineral dependence is diversifiable

Conventional vehicles offer few pathways to reduce fuel dependence; ethanol blending can marginally reduce fuel imports and emissions but is unlikely to eliminate the dependence. Battery technologies, however, can diversify or reduce our import dependence. While imports may be necessary in the near term, the long-term opportunity lies in developing the domestic ecosystem and reducing strategic dependence. Advancements have already reduced the need for critical minerals such as cobalt or nickel, while alternative chemistries such as sodium-ion can reduce dependence on lithium supply chains.

Energy is locally generated

Oil is extracted abroad, priced abroad, and shipped through vulnerable routes outside India’s control. Electricity is generated domestically – with an increasingly diverse mix such as coal, solar, and wind – and priced by Indian regulators. This is the structural advantage of electrification.

Even if EVs account for over 75% of annual vehicle sales by 2040, the resulting electricity demand would represent less than 10% of India's total electricity consumption, a share the grid can absorb. India generates about 30% of its electricity from non-fossil sources, and that share is increasing. As the grid becomes cleaner, the EV fleet automatically becomes cleaner – without altering a single vehicle. This has no equivalent in the oil economy.

EV and battery manufacturing can create jobs

Fuel imports do not significantly stimulate domestic economic activity. By contrast, domestic EV components and battery manufacturing can generate jobs within India. Driven by the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes (for battery cells and EVs) and Viksit Bharat 2047, the EV sector can generate 50 lakh–1 crore direct and indirect jobs by 2040 as per a global study.

In conclusion, battery and mineral imports are not risk-free. But they are a manageable form of dependence: costs are falling, recycling can reduce imports, and domestic industry can grow around them. None of these applies to crude oil.

Having said this, India must act now on the underlying structural gaps to avoid falling into a new dependency trap. Recycling needs immediate attention because the current Battery management rules lack strong enforcement and collection infrastructure. Expanding manufacturing requires sustained PLI support and patient private investments. Indigenous battery chemistries and technologies need stronger university and industry partnerships and public research funding. Skill development must begin now to prepare a workforce for jobs that will become available 2040. The fuel crisis is a warning. Whether India treats this as an emergency or an opportunity depends on the actions it takes in the next five years.

Spurthi Ravuri is a Research Scientist, and Thirumalai NC is Sector Head, Strategic Studies, at the Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP), a research-based think tank.

A Forgotten Industrial Legacy: North Carolina as America's Original Lithium Capital One of the most underappreciated dimensions of USGS lithium in the Carolinas is its historical depth.
Consequently, the case for USGS lithium in the Carolinas as a long-term national asset is difficult to dismiss.
Related analysis on the broader Appalachian lithium assessment programme is available via Metal Tech News at metaltechnews.com.
text:
America's Lithium Blind Spot: Why the Ground Beneath the Carolinas Could Rewrite the Nation's Battery Future

For most of the twentieth century, the story of American mineral dominance was told through coal seams in Appalachia, copper pits in the Southwest, and iron ranges in the Great Lakes. What that story rarely acknowledged was a quieter, less glamorous chapter unfolding in the rolling foothills of North Carolina. That chapter closed in the 1990s, yet a new assessment of USGS lithium in the Carolinas suggests it may be time to reopen it, at a scale that would have been difficult to imagine when the last Carolina lithium mine went dark.

The Geology That Started It All: Understanding Appalachian Pegmatites

Before examining what the USGS has found, it is worth understanding why the southern Appalachians host lithium in the first place. The answer lies in a geological process that unfolded hundreds of millions of years ago during the assembly and subsequent erosion of the ancient supercontinent Pangaea.

As magmatic bodies cooled deep within the crust, the final stages of crystallisation produced highly enriched fluids capable of concentrating elements that do not fit neatly into common rock-forming minerals. Lithium, along with cesium, tantalum, beryllium, and rubidium, was swept into these residual melts and eventually solidified into pegmatites: coarse-grained igneous rocks whose oversized crystal structures are a direct product of slow, volatile-rich cooling.

The Appalachian pegmatite belt runs through the Blue Ridge and Piedmont geological provinces, cutting across both Carolinas in a southwesterly orientation that mirrors the ancient continental collision zones responsible for creating the mountain chain itself. Lithium mineralisation within this belt is primarily hosted in spodumene, a lithium aluminium silicate mineral. Furthermore, spodumene lithium extraction is the same process targeted by the world's largest hard-rock lithium operations in Western Australia's Pilbara and Goldfields regions.

This geological kinship with Western Australian deposits is significant. It suggests that the processing chemistry, metallurgical behaviour, and concentrate quality of Carolina spodumene ore could be broadly comparable to the ore types that global battery supply chains are already equipped to handle — a point that could reduce technical risk for future development programmes.

What the USGS Assessment Actually Measured

The distinction between a USGS mineral resource assessment and a mineable reserve is not merely semantic. It is the difference between a weather forecast and a harvest guarantee, and investors or policymakers who conflate the two risk misreading the significance of this work entirely.

What the USGS produced for the southern Appalachian region is a probabilistic quantitative mineral resource assessment: a scientifically rigorous estimate of how much undiscovered, economically recoverable lithium oxide could plausibly exist within a geologically defined region, based on indirect evidence rather than drill holes.

How the Methodology Was Constructed

The methodology assembled multiple independent data streams:

Regional geologic mapping to identify terrain favourable for pegmatite formation

Geochemical sampling data revealing lithium anomalies at surface and near-surface levels

Geophysical survey integration to model structural controls on pegmatite emplacement at depth

Catalogued records of known mineral occurrences within the study area

Global analogue datasets from lithium pegmatite districts worldwide, used to calibrate deposit size and frequency modelling

The output is expressed as a probability distribution rather than a single number, which is the scientifically honest approach when subsurface geology has not been systematically drilled.

Southern Appalachian Lithium Assessment: Probabilistic Output

Confidence Level Estimated Recoverable Lithium Oxide 90% probability (minimum floor) 60,000 metric tons 50% probability (median estimate) 1.43 million metric tons 10% probability (upside scenario) 6.9 million metric tons

The 90% confidence figure represents the floor: the amount of lithium oxide that USGS geologists are highly confident exists, even under conservative assumptions. The median estimate of 1.43 million metric tons is the central case. The 10% upside of 6.9 million metric tons reflects genuine geological uncertainty on the high end, not wishful thinking.

Critical distinction for investors: These are estimates of undiscovered resources. No drilling has confirmed these deposits individually. Significant exploration investment, resource definition work, environmental review, and feasibility analysis would be required before any of this material could be classified as a mineable reserve under internationally recognised reporting standards such as JORC or NI 43-101.

The Northern Appalachian Piece: Building a Continental Picture

The southern assessment did not emerge in isolation. In April 2026, the USGS released a companion study covering the northern Appalachian region, focused primarily on pegmatite districts in Maine and New Hampshire. That study identified approximately 900,000 metric tons of recoverable lithium oxide in the northern belt.

When combined with the southern assessment, the full Appalachian lithium picture takes shape:

Region Estimated Lithium Oxide Primary States Southern Appalachians 1.43 million metric tons (median) North Carolina, South Carolina Northern Appalachians ~900,000 metric tons Maine, New Hampshire Total Appalachian Region ~2.3 million metric tons Eastern U.S.

At 2025 U.S. import levels, this combined figure represents the theoretical equivalent of more than 328 years of lithium imports replaced by domestic production. Even at the conservative 90% confidence floor for the southern assessment alone, the numbers are strategically significant.

Translating Geology Into Battery Terms: The Real-World Scale of the Carolinas' Lithium Potential

Metric tons of lithium oxide are an abstract unit for most readers. The USGS assessment helpfully translated the median southern Appalachian estimate into application-level equivalents that place the resource in direct economic and technological context.

What 1.43 Million Metric Tons of Lithium Oxide Could Power:

Application Implied Supply Capacity Electric vehicle batteries ~80 million EVs Grid-scale stationary storage systems ~1 million units Laptop computers ~110 billion units (approximately a 600-year supply) Smartphones ~300 billion units (roughly 36 per person alive today)

These figures require important caveats. Lithium demand per battery varies significantly with chemistry, cell format, and energy density. Battery technology is also evolving rapidly, with solid-state and lithium-sulphur chemistries potentially altering lithium consumption per kilowatt-hour of storage. The USGS equivalents are illustrative benchmarks, not production projections.

That said, the order of magnitude is striking. Even if only a fraction of the probabilistic resource were ultimately confirmed and developed, the contribution to U.S. battery supply chain security could be material.

A Forgotten Industrial Legacy: North Carolina as America's Original Lithium Capital

One of the most underappreciated dimensions of USGS lithium in the Carolinas is its historical depth. The region's identity as a lithium producer is not a speculative future scenario. It is a documented industrial reality that the current generation has simply forgotten.

North Carolina's Kings Mountain district and Hallman-Beam mine were active lithium producers long before the electric vehicle transition created the demand environment that now commands front-page attention. These operations extracted spodumene from the same pegmatite system now subject to USGS probabilistic modelling, supplying lithium for:

Specialty ceramics and heat-resistant glass formulations

High-performance lubricating greases used in industrial and aerospace applications

Chemical synthesis applications requiring lithium compounds

At the time these mines operated, the United States held the position of the world's dominant lithium producer. That status was not lost to geological exhaustion. It was lost to economics.

Why the Carolina Mines Closed: A Structural Shift, Not a Resource Depletion

The closure of Kings Mountain and Hallman-Beam in the 1990s reflected a profound restructuring of global lithium supply, not an absence of ore in the ground. Two competing sources fundamentally altered the cost equation:

South American brine operations in Chile and Argentina's Atacama and Puna regions offered lithium at dramatically lower extraction costs. Understanding lithium brines explained helps clarify why evaporation-based brine processing, which requires minimal energy input and leverages free solar evaporation in high-altitude salt flats, simply could not be matched on operating cost by hard-rock spodumene mining in the Carolinas.

Australian hard-rock operations, particularly in Western Australia's Greenbushes and subsequent Pilbara districts, delivered large-scale, low-cost spodumene concentrate that further compressed margins available to U.S. producers.

The result was a broader deindustrialisation of domestic critical mineral production, a pattern now being examined with renewed urgency given the concentration of battery supply chains in geopolitically sensitive regions.

The fact that Carolina lithium deposits were not mined out, but rather priced out, is one of the most strategically important details in the entire USGS assessment narrative. The ore is still there. The question is whether evolving economics, policy priorities, and technology can change the viability calculation.

From Scientific Baseline to Potential Production: The Development Pathway

Understanding where the USGS assessment sits within a full mine development lifecycle is essential for interpreting its significance accurately. The assessment is the beginning of a long journey, not the end of one.

The Staged Pathway from USGS Assessment to Active Mine:

Regional exploration targeting: Geophysical surveys, soil geochemistry, and geological mapping focused on narrowing the highest-priority zones within the assessed area

Resource definition drilling: Systematic diamond core drilling programmes designed to intercept, sample, and characterise individual pegmatite bodies

Mineral resource estimation: Construction of three-dimensional geological models and resource estimates compliant with JORC, NI 43-101, or equivalent reporting codes

Metallurgical testwork: Laboratory and pilot-scale processing trials to determine spodumene recovery rates, concentrate grades, and downstream conversion characteristics

Environmental baseline studies: Multi-year ecological, hydrological, and community impact assessments required to support permitting applications

Permitting and regulatory review: Federal and state environmental review processes, which in the U.S. can span several years depending on land tenure, environmental sensitivity, and community engagement

Feasibility studies: Definitive economic modelling incorporating capital cost estimates, operating cost projections, and lithium price sensitivity analysis

Mine construction and commissioning: Physical development of mine infrastructure, processing facilities, and logistics connections to market

Each stage involves its own capital requirement, timeline, and technical risk. The aggregate timeframe from initial exploration to first production at a new hard-rock lithium operation has historically ranged from ten to twenty years in jurisdictions with complex permitting environments.

The Lithium Supply Chain Vulnerability the Carolinas Assessment Addresses

The strategic backdrop against which the USGS assessment must be read is one of pronounced and well-documented U.S. vulnerability in lithium supply chains. In addition, innovations such as direct lithium extraction technology may eventually alter the economics of domestic production significantly.

U.S. Lithium Supply Chain: Current Position

Metric Status Domestic large-scale lithium mines 1 (Albemarle's Silver Peak, Nevada) Primary import sources South America (Chile, Argentina), Australia Global lithium production growth (past 30 years) More than 40-fold increase Projected global production capacity growth by 2029 Expected to double again Appalachian resource vs. annual U.S. imports Equivalent to 328+ years of replacement

The United States currently relies on a single large-scale domestic lithium mine, Albemarle's Silver Peak operation in Nevada, for the entirety of its domestic hard-rock lithium production. Silver Peak is a brine-based operation, not a spodumene mine, and its output represents a small fraction of U.S. lithium consumption.

The broader context is a global lithium market that has undergone a 40-fold production expansion over the past three decades, almost entirely outside U.S. borders. Projected capacity doublings by 2029 will again be dominated by overseas expansions unless domestic programmes accelerate meaningfully.

Benchmarking the Carolinas Against Global Lithium Geography

Placing the USGS estimates in a global context reveals both the opportunity and the challenge. The Appalachian pegmatite system is geologically credible and historically proven. However, whether it can compete commercially with established global producers is a separate question that exploration and feasibility work will ultimately have to answer.

Note: Direct numerical comparison between brine and hard-rock resources requires lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) conversion and adjustment for differing processing cost structures. Brine operations typically deliver lower operating costs but require substantial evaporation infrastructure. Hard-rock spodumene requires energy-intensive calcination and conversion but can achieve higher lithium recovery rates from ore.

One dimension that favours the Carolinas over many emerging lithium jurisdictions is infrastructure proximity. The region is served by established road and rail networks, sits within reach of major industrial centres, and has an existing workforce with relevant mining and materials processing experience from historical operations. These are factors that do not appear in geological assessments but materially affect the economics of bringing a resource to production.

What the USGS Assessment Signals for the Broader Mineral Security Agenda

The USGS assessment is explicitly positioned within a larger federal mission to characterise domestic mineral potential as the scientific foundation for subsequent policy action. The assessment itself states that mineral science of this kind is the precursor to permitting reform, investment facilitation, and mining workforce development, though none of these downstream outcomes are guaranteed or project-specific commitments.

What the assessment does provide is credibility: a federal scientific imprimatur on the geological potential of a region that could otherwise be dismissed as historically interesting but commercially irrelevant. For exploration companies evaluating where to direct capital, a USGS quantitative assessment of this scale meaningfully de-risks the geological thesis, even while leaving all technical, economic, and regulatory work ahead.

Furthermore, Australia's lithium industry offers a compelling parallel — demonstrating how policy support, investment incentives, and geological confidence can combine to build world-scale production capacity from a strong resource base. The growing recognition of lithium as a tier-one critical mineral, embedded across electric vehicles, grid storage, consumer electronics, military equipment, and aerospace alloys, ensures that the strategic rationale for domestic production development will only intensify as global demand continues its structural climb. Consequently, the case for USGS lithium in the Carolinas as a long-term national asset is difficult to dismiss.

TULARE COUNTY – Agriculture still dominates the list of Tulare County’s most valuable businesses, but a different kind of farm has taken over the top spot.

The Tulare County Assessor’s Office recently released its annual report of the Top 20 businesses in the county, based on the amount of total business property assessment.

Most of the list includes major agriculture operations whose names are familiar both here and internationally, such as California Dairies (No. 2), Setton Pistachio (No. 2), Land O’Lakes (No. 3), Saputo Cheese (Nos. 7 & 15), and Lactalis (No. 10). In fact, 12 of the top 20 businesses are agriculture related businesses, including Ventura Coastal (No. 5), Calgren Dairy Fuels (No. 9), Touchstone Pistachios (No. 11), Treehouse Almonds (No. 12), Porterville Citrus (No. 17) and Western Milling (No. 20).

But the top company in terms of assessed value is an energy company with a massive southern Tulare County solar farm, 20SD 8MW, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of AES Clean Energy. The entity was created to develop and operate the Rexford Solar Farm, a major solar and battery storage project located on a 3,614-acre site in Ducor, California.

The developer 8 Minute Solar, owners of the Rexford 1 Solar Project, is now developing the second phase of the project, or Rexford 2, near the town of Ducor in southeastern Tulare County. Approved by Tulare County in 2020, Rexford 1 was already the largest solar farm in the nation, estimated to generate 700 megawatts (MW) with another 700 MW of battery storage.

Now, with its second phase, 8 Minute Solar — named for the amount of time it takes for the sun’s light to reach the Earth — is building a 500 MW system with 500 MW of storage on 1,200 acres near the original project for a combined 1,200 MW of solar energy and 1,200 MW of storage. The project covers nearly 5,000 acres.

The project is slated to come online between 2027 and 2028.

The list also includes another energy company you may not have heard about. Renewable energy developer Ormat Technologies operates two major utility-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). Bottleneck Energy Storage Facility is an active 80 MW / 320 MWh lithium-ion battery storage facility located in Tulare. It entered commercial operations in October 2024 and operates under a 15-year Power Purchase Agreement.

Ormat also owns the Shirk Energy Storage Project, an active 80 MW / 320 MWh facility located in Tulare. It achieved full commercial operation on March 12, and is backed by a hybrid tax equity partnership with Morgan Stanley Renewables.

The list also includes retail giants Amazon, which has two distribution centers in Visalia and is good enough to be No. 8 on the list; Walmart, which has a major distribution center in Porterville and comes in at No. 16 on the list; and UPS, No. 13 on the list, also with a major statewide logistics warehouse.

There are two food processing companies on the list, Dreyers Ice Cream is No. 14 on the list, and Ruiz Foods, known for manufacturing and processing the El Monterey brand of frozen foods, comes in at No. 14. No. 19 on the list is Banc of America Leasing & Capital, the consumer financing arm of Bank of America.

text:
High gas prices are making low-cost EV leases more attractive to drivers who want to spend less on fuel without committing to buying a new car outright.

Among lease offers from nearly every mainstream automaker, the Kia Niro EV stood out this month as the strongest option for shoppers focused on keeping costs down.

What happened?

The headline numbers are a $239 monthly payment, a 24-month term, and $3,999 due upfront, which works out to an effective cost of about $400 per month before taxes and fees.

According to Electrek's Jo Borrás, citing CarFax's monthly list of the 10 cheapest new-vehicle lease deals in the US, the 2026 Kia Niro EV Wind is the lowest-cost new EV lease available in June 2026.

It was also the only electric vehicle on CarFax's list of best leases this month.

The Niro EV comes with a 201-horsepower electric motor, a 64.8-kilowatt-hour battery, a little more than 250 miles of EPA-estimated range, and 100-kilowatt charging that takes about 40 minutes to go from 10% to 80%.

Why does it matter?

Cost is still one of the main reasons many shoppers hesitate on EVs, even as interest in moving away from gas-powered vehicles grows. And with used EV prices rising along with demand, a cheaper monthly lease can be a more practical way in.

For households that mainly use a car for commuting, errands, school drop-offs, and other local driving, a range of more than 250 miles could be enough for everyday needs.

Because they run on electricity, EVs can reduce or eliminate gas station visits.

They also usually require less routine maintenance than gas vehicles since they have fewer moving parts.

This lease may not be the best match for drivers who often take long trips, but it does offer a path into EV driving without the full cost and ownership uncertainty that can come with buying in a still-developing market.

What can I do?

The advertised monthly payment is only one part of the deal. Before signing, review the full amount due at signing, mileage limits, possible excess wear charges, and the effective monthly cost after fees are added.

Leasing can be a good fit if you want lower upfront costs and like changing vehicles every few years. It may be less appealing if you drive many miles or prefer to keep a car for a long time.

If you are shopping for an EV, think through charging before you sign. Having home charging or dependable access at work or through nearby public chargers can make an EV lease much easier to live with.

Resources like CarFax's monthly lease rankings can also make comparison shopping faster because they account for both the monthly payment and upfront costs, rather than highlighting only one figure.
